subject: session length in multi-session models and heavy-tailed detection functions

messages.author: 1ac467f4b169c2d3
messages.subject: session length in multi-session models and heavy-tailed detection functions
parts:
Hi all, 

I am hoping to use SECR to analyze a large historical dataset of live captures (~2400 total captures, ~580 traps (with varying effort), 850 occasions). I have some questions regarding how to set up my models.

1) The data were collected over multiple years, so I am planning to use multi-session models to meet the closure assumption. I understand that sessions are intended to be independent, but I am struggling with how to define the length of the sessions to best meet that assumption. Of course changing session length alters the number of recaptures in a session. How much does session length and the number of recaptures within a session matter if I am interested in a single estimate of density rather than session-specific estimates? Does having sessions of varying length bias estimates? 

In this study, around 30 traps at a time were generally set for 2 week blocks. However, the data don't break up into nice discrete 2 week blocks, as any given week of trapping might represent week 1 or week 2 at a given trap. Thus there is often some proportion of traps >0% but <100% that were trapped in the previous week, which seems to make it difficult to decide where one session should end and another should begin. Any suggestions on how to define sessions in this scenario?

2) I have some extreme movements in this dataset - the mean is ~1 km but the max is >23 km. Below is a figure showing distances moved, excluding those of 0/recaptures at the same trap to make it easier to see the outliers. The study area here is not geographically constrained like on a small island, aside from a river on one side. I would expect that a long-tailed detection function will better fit the data, but these are not really advised. What is recommended for deciding on buffer width in this case? Is sigma going to be skewed by these long movements?





Thank you!

Laura

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: session length in multi-session models and heavy-tailed detection functions
parts:
Hi Laura
Big questions - this is the most critical stage of any analysis! I assume from other clues that your traps were not really traps, but rather some sort of proximity detector (DNA hair snag, camera?). That gives you more freedom to aggregate data, particularly by collapsing occasions using outputdetector 'count' in reduce.capthist. (reduce(CH, ...). Aggregation makes the problem solvable (580 occasions is too many) without sacrificing anything (except possibly the ability to model day to day variation in detection , but who cares about that?).

1. Short session length does not cause bias, but it reduces the number of recaptures (because recaptures between sessions don't count) and hence reduces the precision of estimates of lambda0 and sigma. That may or may not be critical in your case - it depends on the data.

I assume you specify 'usage' to allow for detectors used/not used on particular occasions. Can't really advise on specifics as they depend on the pattern of use/non-use. If your traps are not really traps then you have a lot more latitude, and can even define notional occasions (secondary sessions) that are asynchronous in real time (Efford Borchers & Mowat 2013 MEE).

2. "long-tailed detection function will better fit the data, but these are not really advised" I guess I am partly responsible for that advice. The worry about long tails is that they potentially make the density estimates dependent on the extent of the habitat mask. You have to be aware of that; it may be inescapable. I have relaxed a bit myself and started using long-tailed detection functions to accommodate occasional extreme movements - may be the lesser of two risks. Can assess impact with your own data. Long movements will result in the fitting of a halfnormal function with larger sigma than if the movements didn't happen, sure; probably that will bias density estimates low, but I doubt it's a big effect in your case. See the usual advice about buffers and habitat masks (secr-habitatmasks.pdf).

Murray

messages.author: 1ac467f4b169c2d3
messages.subject: Re: session length in multi-session models and heavy-tailed detection functions
parts:
Hi Murray,

Thanks very much for your response. The traps in this case are in fact traps, which sounds like it might complicate matters. When trapping occurred at a given location, there were multiple traps set there within a relatively small area, so I was going to consider this a "multi" detector. (Usually only 1 individual captured, but multiple captures were possible and did occur infrequently.) If the 580 traps are too many, is aggregation an appropriate thing to do for true traps? Is there a rule of thumb of what would be considered too many?

Yes, I will have usage included in the trap layout files. Only a small proportion (~30/580) would have been in use at any given time. Usage was variable across sessions, so I'll end up having a separate trap file for each session, and each of those will have usage recorded specific to that session. 

I think the long tail problem will be somewhat inescapable with this dataset. Thanks for your thoughts on this!

Laura

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: session length in multi-session models and heavy-tailed detection functions
parts:
OK - you seem to be on top of it. Were you thinking of a cluster of single-catch traps as one multi-catch trap? That makes sense to me.

My worry about the number of traps just concerns processing time, and keeping the burden of analysis in proportion to the amount of data. Not for me to judge that. 580 may be fine  (no rule of thumb). See ?reduce.traps for aggregating traps (and keep an eye on the resulting usage attribute). If I was tackling this myself I would try a rough-and-ready aggregation and then check that the shortcut was not greatly changing the estimates.

Murray
